<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:converse}
If $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$, must $X$ be uniformly subprojective?
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
Let $H\in\mathcal S(X)$ be uniformly subprojective for its inherited norm with constant $K$, and suppose that $(X,H)$ has the lifting property. Then
\[
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)\ge a_X(H)/K.
\]
If no infinite-dimensional subspace of $H$ is complemented in $X$, then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$.
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
For an infinite-dimensional $\mathcal L_1$-space $X$, over either scalar field, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},nosep]
\item $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$;
\item $X$ is uniformly subprojective;
\item $X$ is subprojective;
\item $X$ contains no infinite-dimensional reflexive subspace.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X)$, with the value $\infty$ allowed. Their common finite value is at most the distortion of any embedding of $X$ into an $L_1(\mu)$.
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- theoremc-1: body_md -->
Let $X$ be H.I. Then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$ under any of the following hypotheses:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},nosep]
\item every strictly singular endomorphism is strictly cosingular;
\item every product of $m$ strictly singular endomorphisms is compact, for some $m\ge1$;
\item the Banach space $\mathcal{SS}(X)/\mathcal K(X)$ is reflexive.
\end{enumerate}
Under \textup{(i)}, for every closed $M$ of infinite dimension and codimension, the identity into the norm $\max\{\varepsilon\|x\|,\operatorname{dist}(x,M)\}$ satisfies $\operatorname{in}=\varepsilon$ and $d_+=1$ for $0<\varepsilon\le1$.
<!-- end theoremc-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:kernel}
For $T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ put $\kappa_\infty(T)=\inf\{\|E\|:\dim\ker(T-E)=\infty\}$. Then $d_+(T)=\kappa_\infty(T)$. More precisely, if $S\notin\Phi_+$ and $\delta>0$, there is a nuclear operator $V$ with $\|V\|<\delta$ and $\dim\ker(S-V)=\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Operators with infinite-dimensional kernel are not in $\Phi_+$, so $d_+\le\kappa_\infty$. Let $S\notin\Phi_+$ with $\dim\ker S<\infty$ (otherwise take $V=0$). Then $S$ is not bounded below on any closed subspace of finite codimension. Put $W_1=X$ and choose a unit vector $x_1$ with $\|Sx_1\|<\delta2^{-3}$. For $n\ge2$, put $W_n=W\cap W_{n-1}$, where $W$ is given by Mazur's device for $\operatorname{span}\{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\}$ with parameter $1/2$, and choose a unit vector $x_n\in W_n$ with $\|Sx_n\|<\delta2^{-n-2}$. Since $x_{m+1},\dots,x_n\in W_{m+1}$, we have $\|\sum_{k\le m}a_kx_k\|\le2\|\sum_{k\le n}a_kx_k\|$ for $m<n$. Thus $(x_n)$ is basic with constant at most $2$, its biorthogonal functionals have norm at most $4$, and by the Hahn--Banach theorem they extend to $f_n\in X^*$ with $\|f_n\|\le4$ and $f_n(x_m)=\delta_{nm}$. The operator $V=\sum_n f_n\otimes Sx_n$ is nuclear, $\|V\|<\delta$, and $(S-V)x_m=0$ for all $m$. For general $T$ and $\eta>d_+(T)$, apply this to $S=T-E$ with $\|E\|<\eta$ and $T-E\notin\Phi_+$; then $\kappa_\infty(T)\le\|E+V\|<\eta+\delta$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:extension}
For every $T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$,
\[
d_+(T)=\inf_{M\in \mathcal S(X)}\operatorname{ext}_X(T|_M).
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If $E$ extends $T|_M$, then $M\subset\ker(T-E)$; conversely, if $\dim\ker(T-E)=\infty$, then $E$ extends $T|_M$ for $M=\ker(T-E)$. So the right-hand side is $\kappa_\infty(T)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:subproj}
If $X$ is uniformly subprojective with constant $\lambda$, or if $Y$ is $\lambda$-injective, then $\operatorname{in}(T)\le d_+(T)\le\lambda\operatorname{in}(T)$ for $T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$. Hence $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)\le\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X)$. Moreover $\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X)=1$, and so $d_+=\operatorname{in}$, when $X$ is a Hilbert space, $\ell_p(\Gamma)$ with $1\le p<\infty$, or $c_0(\Gamma)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
If $E|_M=T|_M$ then $\|T|_M\|\le\|E\|$, which gives the left inequality. For the right one fix $M\in\mathcal S(X)$. In the first case choose $N\in\mathcal S(M)$ and a projection $P$ of $X$ onto $N$ with $\|P\|\le\lambda$; then $TP$ extends $T|_N$ and $\|TP\|\le\lambda\|T|_M\|$. In the second case extend $T|_M$ with norm at most $\lambda\|T|_M\|$. Proposition~\ref{prop:extension} gives $d_+(T)\le\lambda\|T|_M\|$.

Hilbert spaces have constant $1$. Let $X=\ell_p$ ($1\le p<\infty$) or $c_0$ with unit vector basis $(e_k)$, $M\in\mathcal S(X)$, $0<\theta<1$. Put $n_0=0$ and choose inductively unit vectors $y_k\in M$ vanishing on the first $n_{k-1}$ coordinates and integers $n_k>n_{k-1}$ such that the tail of $y_k$ beyond $n_k$ has norm at most $\theta2^{-k-3}$. Let $u_k$ be the normalized restriction of $y_k$ to $(n_{k-1},n_k]$; then $\|y_k-u_k\|\le\theta2^{-k-2}$. With $u_k^*$ the norm-one functional supported on the same block and $u_k^*(u_k)=1$, $Px=\sum_ku_k^*(x)u_k$ is a projection of norm one onto $[u_k]$. The operator $U=I+\sum_ku_k^*\otimes(y_k-u_k)$ satisfies $\|U-I\|\le\theta$ and $Uu_k=y_k$, so $UPU^{-1}$ is a projection onto $[y_k]\subset M$ of norm at most $(1+\theta)/(1-\theta)$. For $\ell_p(\Gamma)$ and $c_0(\Gamma)$, a separable $M_0\in\mathcal S(M)$ is supported by a countable $\Gamma_0$, and $\ell_p(\Gamma_0)$, $c_0(\Gamma_0)$ are $1$-complemented by restriction.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite}
If $R:X\to Y$ has finite rank, then $\operatorname{in}(T+R)=\operatorname{in}(T)$ and $d_+(T+R)=d_+(T)$. If $F$ is finite-dimensional and $i:Y\to Y\oplus_\infty F$ is the inclusion, then $\operatorname{in}(iT)=\operatorname{in}(T)$ and $d_+^{X,Y\oplus_\infty F}(iT)=d_+^{X,Y}(T)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Applying the finite-codimensional criterion on subspaces of $\ker R$ shows $T+R\in\Phi_+\iff T\in\Phi_+$, so translation by $R$ preserves the complement of $\Phi_+$. For $M\in\mathcal S(X)$, $\operatorname{in}(T)\le\|T|_{M\cap\ker R}\|\le\|(T+R)|_M\|$; take the infimum and exchange $T$ and $T+R$. A perturbation $B=(B_1,B_2):X\to Y\oplus_\infty F$ has $B_2$ of finite rank and $\|B_1\|\le\|B\|$, so $iT-B\in\Phi_+\iff T-B_1\in\Phi_+$; perturbations $iD$ give the reverse inequality. The statement on $\operatorname{in}$ follows from the isometric inclusion.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:renorm}
For $C\ge1$, the inequality $d_+^{X,Y}(T)\le C\operatorname{in}(T)$ holds for all $Y$ and $T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ if and only if it holds for all identities $J_{|\cdot|}$ into equivalent renormings of $X$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:renorm}
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\sup_{|\cdot|\sim\|\cdot\|}\frac{d_+(J_{|\cdot|})}{\operatorname{in}(J_{|\cdot|})}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $T\in\Phi_+(X,Y)$ (otherwise $d_+(T)=0$), let $P_0$ be a projection onto $\ker T$, and define $T'x=(Tx,P_0x)\in E=Y\oplus_\infty\ker T$. If $\|w\|\le c\|Tw\|$ on $\ker P_0$, then $\|x\|\le(c+1)\|T'x\|$, so $Z=T'(X)$ is closed and $S:X\to Z$, $Sx=T'x$, is an isomorphism onto. By Lemma~\ref{lem:finite}, $\operatorname{in}(S)=\operatorname{in}(T)$ and $d_+^{X,E}(T')=d_+^{X,Y}(T)$. An operator with values in $Z$ is upper semi-Fredholm into $Z$ if and only if it is so into $E$, hence $d_+^{X,Y}(T)=d_+^{X,E}(T')\le d_+^{X,Z}(S)$. Finally $|x|=\|Sx\|$ is an equivalent norm, $S=UJ_{|\cdot|}$ with $U$ a surjective isometry, and composition with $U$ preserves $d_+$ and $\operatorname{in}$. The identity of $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ has $\operatorname{in}=d_+=1$, so the supremum is at least $1$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:complemented-inheritance}
If $H$ is a closed infinite-dimensional complemented subspace of $X$, with its inherited norm, then
\[
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(H)\le\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X).
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Choose a bounded projection $P$ onto $H$, write $Z=\ker P$, and for $T:H\to Y$ and $t>0$ define
\[
 T_tx=(TPx,t(I-P)x)\in Y\oplus_\infty Z.
\]
Then $\operatorname{in}(T_t)\le\operatorname{in}(T)$. For a perturbation $E:X\to Y\oplus_\infty Z$ of norm $r<t$, all four blocks obtained by restricting to $H$ or $Z$ and projecting on target coordinates have norm at most $r$. The block $D=tI_Z-E_{22}$ is invertible and $\|D^{-1}\|\le(t-r)^{-1}$. Triangular elimination shows that $T_t-E$ is upper semi-Fredholm if and only if its Schur complement
\[
 T-E_{11}-E_{12}D^{-1}E_{21}
\]
is upper semi-Fredholm. If it is not, then $d_+^{H,Y}(T)\le r+r^2/(t-r)$. Perturbations with $r\ge t$ also satisfy the resulting lower bound, so
\[
 d_+^{X,Y\oplus_\infty Z}(T_t)
 \ge\frac{t\,d_+^{H,Y}(T)}{t+d_+^{H,Y}(T)}.
\]
If $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=C<\infty$, combine this with $d_+(T_t)\le C\operatorname{in}(T_t)\le C\operatorname{in}(T)$ and let $t\to\infty$. The case $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$ is immediate.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:key}
Let $H\in\mathcal S(X)$ be uniformly subprojective with constant $K$, and let $C$ be a lifting constant of $(X,H)$. Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $0<r<1/C$, and put
\[
 \theta=\frac{KCr\,(r/\varepsilon+Cr)}{1-Cr}.
\]
If $d_+(J_\varepsilon)<r$ and $\theta<1$, then some $N\in\mathcal S(H)$ satisfies
\[
 \lambda_X(N)\le\frac{K\,(r/\varepsilon+Cr)}{1-\theta}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:extension} there are $M\in\mathcal S(X)$ and $E\in\mathcal L(X,X_\varepsilon)$ with $E|_M=J_\varepsilon|_M$ and $|Ex|_\varepsilon\le r\|x\|$ for all $x$. Regard $E$ as an operator on $X$. Then $Ex=x$ for $x\in M$, and by \eqref{eq:norm-eps}
\[
 \|E\|\le r/\varepsilon,\qquad \|q_HE\|\le r.
\]
Let $L\in\mathcal L(X)$ be a lifting of $q_HE$ with $\|L\|\le Cr$, and put $A=E-L$. Then $q_HA=0$, so $A$ maps $X$ into $H$, and $\|A\|\le r/\varepsilon+Cr$. For $x\in M$ we have $Ax=x-Lx$ and $\|Ax\|\ge(1-Cr)\|x\|$; hence $A(M)$ is a closed infinite-dimensional subspace of $H$. Choose $N\in\mathcal S(A(M))$ and a projection $Q$ of $H$ onto $N$ with $\|Q\|\le K$.

Let $y\in N$ and write $y=Ax$ with $x\in M$, so that $\|x\|\le\|y\|/(1-Cr)$. Since $Ax=x-Lx$,
\[
 Ay=A(x-Lx)=y-ALx,\qquad QAy=y-QALx,
\]
and $\|QALx\|\le K\|A\|\,Cr\,\|x\|\le\theta\|y\|$. Thus $B=QA|_N\in\mathcal L(N)$ satisfies $\|B-I_N\|\le\theta<1$, so $B$ is invertible with $\|B^{-1}\|\le(1-\theta)^{-1}$. The operator $R=B^{-1}QA:X\to N$ satisfies $Ry=y$ for $y\in N$; it is a projection of $X$ onto $N$ with $\|R\|\le K(r/\varepsilon+Cr)/(1-\theta)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:lifting}
Let $H\in\mathcal S(X)$ be uniformly subprojective with an admissible constant $K$, and suppose that $(X,H)$ has the lifting property, with lifting constant $C$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $\displaystyle\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\frac{d_+(J_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\ge\frac{a_X(H)}{K}$, and consequently $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)\ge a_X(H)/K$;
\item if $a_X(H)=\infty$, then, for $0<\varepsilon\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:root}
 d_+(J_\varepsilon)\ge r_\varepsilon
 :=\frac{2}{C+\sqrt{C^2+4KC(\varepsilon^{-1}+C)}}.
\end{equation}
In particular $\operatorname{in}(J_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sqrt}
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\frac{d_+(J_\varepsilon)}{\sqrt\varepsilon}
 \ge\frac1{\sqrt{KC}},\qquad
 \frac{d_+(J_\varepsilon)}{\operatorname{in}(J_\varepsilon)}\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For (b), the conditions $Cr<1$ and $\theta<1$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:key} are both satisfied when
\[
 KC(\varepsilon^{-1}+C)r^2+Cr<1.
\]
The positive root of the corresponding equation is $r_\varepsilon$. If $0<r<r_\varepsilon$ and $d_+(J_\varepsilon)<r$, the lemma produces a complemented infinite-dimensional subspace of $H$, contrary to $a_X(H)=\infty$. Letting $r\uparrow r_\varepsilon$ proves \eqref{eq:root}, and its asymptotics give \eqref{eq:sqrt}.

For (a), we may by (b) assume $a=a_X(H)<\infty$. Fix $0<c<a/K$ and put $r=c\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$,
\[
 Cr\to0,\quad
 \theta=\frac{KCc\varepsilon(c+Cc\varepsilon)}{1-Cc\varepsilon}\to0,\quad
 \frac{K(c+Cc\varepsilon)}{1-\theta}\to Kc<a.
\]
For small $\varepsilon$, the inequality $d_+(J_\varepsilon)<c\varepsilon$ would give an $N\in\mathcal S(H)$ with $\lambda_X(N)<a$, which is impossible. Thus $d_+(J_\varepsilon)\ge c\varepsilon$ for small $\varepsilon$, and $c<a/K$ was arbitrary. Use \eqref{eq:in-eps} and Theorem~\ref{thm:renorm} to obtain the bound for $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite-obstruction}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:lifting}, suppose $a=a_X(H)<\infty$, and put $b_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}+C$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-root}
 d_+(J_\varepsilon)\ge
 \rho_\varepsilon(a):=
 \frac{2a}{aC+Kb_\varepsilon+
 \sqrt{(aC+Kb_\varepsilon)^2+4aKC b_\varepsilon(a-1)}}.
\end{equation}
Moreover $\rho_\varepsilon(a)/\varepsilon\to a/K$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and $\rho_\varepsilon(a)\to r_\varepsilon$ as $a\to\infty$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We have $a\ge1$. For $r<r_\varepsilon$, Lemma~\ref{lem:key}, if applicable, gives
\[
 a\le \frac{K b_\varepsilon r(1-Cr)}
 {1-Cr-KC b_\varepsilon r^2}.
\]
Since the denominator is positive, this implies
\[
 a\le(aC+Kb_\varepsilon)r+KC b_\varepsilon(a-1)r^2.
\]
The positive solution of equality is $\rho_\varepsilon(a)$ (also when $a=1$). It is strictly smaller than $r_\varepsilon$, as is seen by substituting $r_\varepsilon$ into the last polynomial. Therefore $d_+(J_\varepsilon)<\rho_\varepsilon(a)$ would allow an $r$ strictly between these numbers and contradict that inequality. The limits follow from the displayed formula.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:complemented}
If $H\in\mathcal S(X)$ is complemented in $X$ and uniformly subprojective for its inherited norm, then $a_X(H)\le\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(H)\,\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)$. In particular, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)\ge a_X(H)$ whenever $H$ is a complemented subspace isometric to a Hilbert space, and this bound is attained on Hilbert spaces.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:lifting}(a) with every admissible $K>\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(H)$. On a Hilbert space both sides equal $1$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:embedding}
Every $\mathcal L_1$-space admits an isomorphic embedding $u:X\to L_1(\mu)$ of finite distortion $D=\|u\|\|u^{-1}|_{u(X)}\|$. One may take $D\le\sigma$ for every strictly admissible local constant $\sigma$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let the index set consist of all finite-dimensional local subspaces $F$, each equipped with a chosen isomorphism $U_F:F\to\ell_1^{\dim F}$ normalized so that
\[
 \|x\|\le\|U_Fx\|_1\le\sigma\|x\|\qquad(x\in F).
\]
Choose an ultrafilter containing all sets $\{F:F\supset F_0\}$, for finite-dimensional $F_0\subset X$. In the Banach-space ultraproduct of the spaces $\ell_1^{\dim F}$, define
\[
 ux=[(z_F(x))_F],\qquad z_F(x)=
 \begin{cases}U_Fx,&x\in F,\\0,&x\notin F.\end{cases}
\]
The map is linear because every finite set of vectors lies in the same $F$ on a set belonging to the ultrafilter; the two norm inequalities pass to the ultralimit. The Banach-lattice ultraproduct is an abstract $L_1$ lattice: its norm is additive on the positive cone. Kakutani's representation theorem \cite{Kak41} identifies it isometrically with an $L_1(\mu)$. Over $\mathbb C$, take the ultraproduct as a complex Banach lattice and apply the representation to its associated real lattice; its complexification gives complex $L_1(\mu)$. This proves the assertion without a separability assumption.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:contractive-lifting}
Let $F$ be an $\mathcal L_1$-space with a strictly admissible local constant $\sigma$, and let $H$ be a reflexive closed subspace of $Y$. Every $T:F\to Y/H$ has a lifting $L:F\to Y$ with $\|L\|\le\sigma\|T\|$. If $F=L_1(\mu)$, the lifting can be chosen with $\|L\|=\|T\|$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This is the reflexive-kernel version of the proof in \cite[Proposition 2.1]{KP97}. A reflexive subspace is proximinal: a bounded minimizing sequence in an affine fiber of $q_H$ has a weakly convergent subsequence after translation into $H$, and the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous. Thus each $e\in Y/H$ has a representative of norm $\|e\|$.

For a finite-dimensional local subspace $E\subset F$, choose $U:E\to\ell_1^{\dim E}$ with $\|U^{-1}\|\le1$ and $\|U\|\le\sigma$. Lift each $TU^{-1}e_j$ to a representative $y_j$ of the same norm. Then
\[
 L_Ex=\sum_j(Ux)_j y_j,\qquad
 q_HL_E=T|_E,\qquad \|L_E\|\le\sigma\|T\|.
\]
For each $f\in F$ the set
\[
 K_f=\{y\in Y:q_Hy=Tf,\ \|y\|\le\sigma\|T\|\|f\|\}
\]
is nonempty and weakly compact: after translating a fiber representative, it is a bounded weakly closed subset of the reflexive space $H$. In the compact product $\prod_{f\in F}K_f$, impose all the closed conditions of additivity and scalar homogeneity. Every finite collection of conditions is satisfied by some $L_E$, because one local subspace $E$ contains all vectors involved. The finite intersection property gives a linear lifting with the required norm bound.

For $F=L_1(\mu)$, every $\sigma>1$ is an admissible local constant. Take such liftings with $\sigma\downarrow1$ and a cluster point in the product of the weakly compact fibers with bound $2\|T\|\|f\|$. The limit is linear and has norm at most $\|T\|$. The reverse inequality follows from $\|q_H\|\le1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:noreflexive}
No infinite-dimensional reflexive subspace of an $\mathcal L_1$-space is complemented. Every infinite-dimensional reflexive subspace $R$ of such a space contains a subspace $H$ isomorphic to $\ell_r$ for some $1<r\le2$. Thus $H$ is internally uniformly subprojective and $a_X(H)=\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
If $P:X\to N$ is a projection onto a reflexive subspace, it is weakly compact, hence completely continuous. Its restriction to $N$ is the identity. Every bounded sequence in $N$ has a weakly convergent subsequence, which is then norm convergent. The unit ball of $N$ is therefore compact, and $N$ is finite-dimensional.

For real scalars, apply the theorem of Aldous to an infinite-dimensional separable subspace of $u(R)\subset L_1(\mu)$: it contains a copy of $\ell_r$, $1\le r\le2$ \cite{Ald81}; proofs are given in \cite{Mau80,Kri80}. Reflexivity excludes $r=1$. A separable subspace of any $L_1(\mu)$ is supported on a countable union of finite-measure sets; multiplying by a positive integrable density and restricting to a countably generated sigma algebra reduces the statement to a separable probability $L_1$ space, which embeds isometrically into $L_1(0,1)$.

For completeness, the real extraction theorem gives the same conclusion over $\mathbb C$. The underlying real space of complex $L_1(\mu)$ embeds into real $L_1(\mu\times\mathbb T)$ by
\[
 f\longmapsto \bigl((\omega,t)\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(e^{it}f(\omega))\bigr),
\]
whose norm is $2\|f\|_1/\pi$ for normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T$. We obtain a real embedding $U:\ell_r(\mathbb R)\to R$. Write $\overline R$ for the conjugate Banach space. The map
\[
 W:\ell_r(\mathbb C)\longrightarrow R\oplus_\infty\overline R,
 \qquad W(a+ib)=(Ua+iUb,\ Ua-iUb)
\]
is complex linear and bounded below: both $Ua$ and $Ub$ are recovered from its coordinates, so
\[
 \|a+ib\|_r\le\|a\|_r+\|b\|_r
 \le2\|U^{-1}\|\,\|W(a+ib)\|.
\]
The two coordinate operators cannot both be strictly singular, since strictly singular operators form an operator ideal closed under addition \cite[Section IV.5]{Kat}. One coordinate is bounded below on an infinite-dimensional complex subspace of $\ell_r$. The gliding-hump construction in Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj} shows that every such subspace contains a copy of complex $\ell_r$. Consequently $R$ or $\overline R$ contains this copy; since $\ell_r$ is isometric to its conjugate, $R$ contains one in either case.

Transport this copy back to $X$. Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj} and isomorphism invariance give a finite internal subprojectivity constant for $H$. Every infinite-dimensional subspace of $H$ is reflexive, so the first paragraph gives $a_X(H)=\infty$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:James}
If a Banach space contains a copy of $\ell_1$, then for every $t>1$ it contains a subspace $W$ with $d(W,\ell_1)<t$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We recall the block argument underlying James' non-distortion theorem \cite{Jam64}. Let $U:\ell_1\to X$ be an embedding and put
\[
 b_n=\inf\{\|Uz\|:\|z\|_1=1,\ \operatorname{supp}z\subset[n,\infty)\},
 \qquad b=\lim_n b_n>0.
\]
Choose $n_0$ and $\delta>0$ with $(b+\delta)/b_{n_0}<t$. Successively choose finitely supported unit vectors $z_k$, with disjoint supports after $n_0$, such that $\|Uz_k\|<b+\delta$. This is possible on every tail by the definition of $b_n$ and density of finite supports. For finitely supported scalar sequences,
\[
 b_{n_0}\sum_k|a_k|\le\Big\|\sum_k a_kUz_k\Big\|
 \le(b+\delta)\sum_k|a_k|.
\]
The closed span of the $Uz_k$ has the required distortion. The argument works over both scalar fields and for the given norm of $X$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:saturation}
Suppose that $u:X\to L_1(\mu)$ is an embedding of distortion $D$ and that $X$ contains no infinite-dimensional reflexive subspace. Then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X)\le D$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Every $M\in\mathcal S(X)$ contains $\ell_1$. Indeed, if it did not, Rosenthal's theorem \cite{Ros74} would give a weakly Cauchy subsequence of every bounded sequence in $M$. Weak sequential completeness would make that subsequence weakly convergent; by the Eberlein--\v Smulian theorem, $M$ would be reflexive, a contradiction. For complex scalars one can apply the real theorem: a real copy of $\ell_1$ yields a complex copy by the conjugate-space argument in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:noreflexive}, now with $r=1$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:James} in $u(M)$ with its ambient $L_1$ norm to obtain a $W\subset u(M)$ with $d(W,\ell_1)<t$, where $1<t<4/3$. The proof of Dor's projection theorem \cite{Dor75} given by Maurey \cite[pp.~XXI.7--XXI.9]{Mau75} gives a projection $Q:L_1(\mu)\to W$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dor}
 \|Q\|\le B(t):=\frac{t^2}{4-3t}.
\end{equation}
Here is how this sufficient bound enters. The finite-dimensional estimate in that proof is $C(t)=t/(4-3t)$, uniformly in the dimension. Taking a weak-star ultralimit of the projections onto the spans of the first $n$ vectors gives an operator $L_1(\mu)\to W^{**}$ of norm at most $C(t)$ which is the identity on $W$. Transporting the canonical norm-one projection $\ell_1^{**}\to\ell_1$ by an isomorphism of distortion less than $t$ gives a projection $W^{**}\to W$ of norm less than $t$. Their composition gives \eqref{eq:Dor}. The bound applies to real and complex scalars; optimal constants are not needed.

Thus $u^{-1}Qu:X\to u^{-1}(W)\subset M$ is a projection of norm at most $DB(t)$. Since $B(t)\to1$ as $t\downarrow1$, we have $a_X(M)\le D$ for every $M$, and \eqref{eq:usp-def} proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:L1}
For an infinite-dimensional $\mathcal L_1$-space $X$, over either scalar field, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},nosep]
\item $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$;
\item $\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X)<\infty$;
\item $X$ is subprojective;
\item $X$ contains no infinite-dimensional reflexive subspace.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, with the value $\infty$ allowed,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L1-equality}
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X).
\end{equation}
If these constants are finite, their common value is at most the distortion of any embedding of $X$ into an $L_1(\mu)$, hence at most every strictly admissible local $\mathcal L_1$ constant. If they are infinite, there is an $H\subset X$ for which the identities in \eqref{eq:norm-eps} satisfy \eqref{eq:root} and \eqref{eq:sqrt}.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj}, and (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is immediate. For (iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv), subprojectivity applied to an infinite-dimensional reflexive subspace would produce such a subspace complemented in $X$, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:noreflexive}. For (iv)$\Rightarrow$(ii), combine Lemmas~\ref{lem:embedding} and \ref{lem:saturation}.

For (i)$\Rightarrow$(iv), suppose $R\in\mathcal S(X)$ is reflexive. Lemma~\ref{lem:noreflexive} gives $H\subset R$, isomorphic to $\ell_r$ for some $1<r\le2$, with a finite admissible internal constant $K$ and $a_X(H)=\infty$. In the lifting principle of \cite[Proposition 2.1]{KP97}, take $F=Y=X$, $E=X/H$, and $Q=q_H$. Its kernel $H$ is reflexive, hence complemented in $H^{**}$ by the identity. Thus $(X,H)$ has the lifting property. Theorem~\ref{thm:lifting}(b) gives $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$, a contradiction, and also gives the stated quantitative obstruction when (iv) fails.

It remains to prove \eqref{eq:L1-equality} in the finite case. Every $M\in\mathcal S(X)$ contains $\ell_1$ by the first paragraph of Lemma~\ref{lem:saturation}. Fix $\eta>0$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:James}, this time with the original norm of $X$, to find $H\in\mathcal S(M)$ with $d(H,\ell_1)<1+\eta$. Then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(H)<1+\eta$. Since $X$ is subprojective, some $N\in\mathcal S(H)$ is complemented in $X$. Heredity of the internal constant gives $\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(N)\le\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(H)<1+\eta$. Corollary~\ref{cor:complemented} now yields
\[
 a_X(M)\le a_X(N)\le\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(N)\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)
 \le(1+\eta)\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X).
\]
Take the supremum over $M$ and let $\eta\downarrow0$. The reverse inequality is Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj}. The bound by the embedding distortion is Lemma~\ref{lem:saturation}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:L1mu}
If $L_1(\mu)$ is infinite-dimensional and isometric to $\ell_1(\Gamma)$, then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(L_1(\mu))=1$. If $\mu$ has a non-atomic measurable set of finite positive measure, then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(L_1(\mu))=\infty$. In particular, for a semi-finite measure $\mu$,
\[
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(L_1(\mu))=
 \begin{cases}1,&\mu\text{ is purely atomic},\\
 \infty,&\mu\text{ is not purely atomic}.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The first case follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj} and $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}\ge1$. On a non-atomic finite-measure set, successive bisections produce an independent sequence of Rademacher functions. The Khintchine inequalities show that their closed span in $L_1$ is isomorphic to $\ell_2$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:L1} gives the second case. The same conclusion holds for complex scalars. For semi-finite measures, the atomic part gives an $\ell_1(\Gamma)$ space, while failure of pure atomicity provides a non-atomic finite-measure part.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:L1explicit}
Let $G\subset L_1(0,1)$ be the closed span of independent standard Gaussian variables, circular complex Gaussian variables over $\mathbb C$. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, put
\[
 |f|_\varepsilon=\max\{\varepsilon\|f\|_1,\ \operatorname{dist}(f,G)\}.
\]
The identity $J_\varepsilon:L_1\to(L_1,|\cdot|_\varepsilon)$ satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{in}(J_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon,\qquad
 d_+(J_\varepsilon)\ge
 \frac{2}{1+\sqrt{5+4\varepsilon^{-1}}}.
\]
Consequently $\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}d_+(J_\varepsilon)/\sqrt\varepsilon\ge1$ and $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(L_1(0,1))=\infty$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Gaussian rotation invariance gives
$\|\sum a_ng_n\|_1=\gamma(\sum|a_n|^2)^{1/2}$, where $\gamma=\|g_1\|_1$. Thus $G$ is a Hilbert space with its inherited norm and admits the internal constant $K=1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:noreflexive} gives $a_{L_1}(G)=\infty$. Since $G$ is reflexive, Lemma~\ref{lem:contractive-lifting} gives the lifting constant $C=1$. Now use Theorem~\ref{thm:lifting}(b).
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The square-root lower bound follows from the quadratic term in Lemma~\ref{lem:key}. No matching upper bound is established here; the exact asymptotic size of this radius remains a question.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:conditional}
Suppose there is $K<\infty$ such that every $M\in\mathcal S(X)$ contains an $H\in\mathcal S(M)$ that is uniformly subprojective with constant $K$ and such that $(X,H)$ has the lifting property. Then
\[
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)\le\Lambda_{\mathrm{usp}}(X)\le K\,\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
If $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$, the right inequality is automatic. Otherwise, for such $H\subset M$, Theorem~\ref{thm:lifting}(a) gives $a_X(M)\le a_X(H)\le K\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)$. Take the supremum over $M$ and use \eqref{eq:usp-def} and Proposition~\ref{prop:subproj}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:Lpn}
Let $2<p_1<p_2<\cdots$ with $p_n\to\infty$, and let $X=(\bigoplus_nL_{p_n}(0,1))_{\ell_2}$ be the real $\ell_2$-sum. Then $X$ is subprojective and $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Subprojectivity is \cite[Proposition 2.1 and Remark 2.11]{OiSp15}. For $p>2$ let $G_p\subset L_p(0,1)$ be the closed span of independent standard Gaussian variables $(g_n)$. Then $\|\sum a_ng_n\|_p=\gamma_p(\sum|a_n|^2)^{1/2}$, and $Pf=\sum_n\langle f,g_n\rangle g_n$ is bounded with $\|Pf\|_p\le\gamma_p\|f\|_2\le\gamma_p\|f\|_p$ and is a projection onto $G_p$, so $G_p$ is a complemented Hilbertian subspace. The Gaussian projection estimate recorded in \cite[Remark 2.11]{OiSp15}, which attributes the estimate to Gordon--Lewis--Retherford \cite{GLR73}, says that every projection of $L_p$ onto $G_p$ has norm at least $c_*\sqrt p$, with $c_*>0$ absolute. The same holds for each $H_0\in\mathcal S(G_p)$: an $L_2$-orthonormal basis $(h_n)$ of $H_0$ consists of independent standard Gaussian variables, the pair $(L_p(\sigma(h_n)),H_0)$ is isometric to $(L_p,G_p)$, and the conditional expectation onto $L_p(\sigma(h_n))$ has norm one. Placing $G_{p_n}$ in the $n$th coordinate of $X$ we get $a_X(G_{p_n})\ge c_*\sqrt{p_n}$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:complemented} gives $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)\ge c_*\sqrt{p_n}$ for all $n$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:HI-restriction}
If $X$ is H.I., then $\operatorname{in}(T|_M)=\operatorname{in}(T)$ for every $T:X\to Y$ and every $M\in\mathcal S(X)$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Only $\operatorname{in}(T|_M)\le\operatorname{in}(T)$ needs proof. Fix $A\in\mathcal S(X)$ and $\delta>0$. Since $q_A:X\to X/A$ has infinite-dimensional kernel, \eqref{eq:HI-distance} makes it strictly singular. Choose $N\in\mathcal S(M)$ with $\|q_A|_N\|<\delta$. For each $x\in N$, choose $y\in A$ with $\|x-y\|\le\delta\|x\|$. Then
\[
 \|Tx\|\le[\|T|_A\|+\delta(\|T|_A\|+\|T\|)]\|x\|.
\]
Let $\delta\downarrow0$ and take the infimum over $A$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:HI-endomorphisms}
On a complex H.I. space, every endomorphism has a unique representation $T=\lambda I+S$, $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$, and
\[
 d_+^{X,X}(T)=\operatorname{in}(T)=|\lambda|.
\]
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The representation is the complex H.I. operator theorem \cite{GoMa93,G07}. The small-restriction property gives $\operatorname{in}(R+S)=\operatorname{in}(R)$ for strictly singular $S$. Strictly singular perturbations preserve upper semi-Fredholmness \cite[Section IV.5]{Kat}, so translation by $S$ also preserves $d_+$. Finally $\operatorname{in}(\lambda I)=d_+(\lambda I)=|\lambda|$, by the Neumann series and the perturbation $\lambda I$ itself.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:HI-graph}
For an H.I. domain,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HI-exact}
 \operatorname{in}(J_{\varepsilon,Q})=\varepsilon,
 \qquad d_+(J_{\varepsilon,Q})=
 \inf_{S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)}\max\{\varepsilon\|I-S\|,\|Q-QS\|\}.
\end{equation}
For a fixed $Q$, the ratios $d_+(J_{\varepsilon,Q})/\varepsilon$ are bounded if and only if there are $S_n\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$ such that
\[
 \sup_n\|I-S_n\|<\infty,\qquad \|Q-QS_n\|\longrightarrow0.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The floor gives $\operatorname{in}\ge\varepsilon$, and the small-restriction property gives an infinite-dimensional subspace where the new norm equals $\varepsilon\|\cdot\|$. Equivalent target norms preserve strict singularity. Thus \eqref{eq:HI-distance} gives the infimum, since
\[
 \|J_{\varepsilon,Q}-S\|_{X\to X_{\varepsilon,Q}}
 =\max\{\varepsilon\|I-S\|,\|Q(I-S)\|\}.
\]
If the ratios have bound $C$, use $\varepsilon=1/n$ to choose $S_n$ with $\|I-S_n\|<C+1/n$ and $\|Q-QS_n\|<(C+1/n)/n$. Conversely, if $\|I-S_n\|\le A$, choose $n$ with $\|Q-QS_n\|\le A\varepsilon$ and use the formula.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:HI-quotients}
For every H.I. space $X$, with $\infty$ allowed,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HI-b}
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\sup_{M\in\mathcal S(X)}b_X(M).
\end{equation}
In particular, finiteness is equivalent to the existence of one $C<\infty$ such that every $M\in\mathcal S(X)$ has a sequence as in \eqref{eq:HI-bdef} with $\sup_n\|I-S_n\|\le C$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
If $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=C_0<\infty$, use Proposition~\ref{prop:HI-graph} with $Q=q_M$ and $\varepsilon=1/n$. The quotient is strictly singular by \eqref{eq:HI-distance}. The resulting sequence satisfies
\[
 \|I-S_n\|<C_0+1/n,\qquad \|q_M(I-S_n)\|<(C_0+1/n)/n.
\]
Hence $b_X(M)\le C_0$.

Conversely, suppose $B=\sup_M b_X(M)<\infty$. Fix $T:X\to Y$, $M\in\mathcal S(X)$ and $\delta>0$. Choose $R_n=I-S_n$ with $\limsup\|R_n\|\le b_X(M)+\delta$ and $a_n=\|q_MR_n\|\to0$. For each $x$, choose $m\in M$ such that $\|R_nx-m\|\le(a_n+1/n)\|x\|$. No linear selection is needed. It follows that
\[
 \|TR_n\|\le\|T|_M\|\|R_n\|
 +(\|T|_M\|+\|T\|)(a_n+1/n).
\]
Since $TS_n$ is strictly singular, $d_+(T)\le\|TR_n\|$ by \eqref{eq:HI-distance}. Take the limit, let $\delta\downarrow0$, and then take the infimum over $M$. This gives $d_+(T)\le B\operatorname{in}(T)$. The two implications also prove \eqref{eq:HI-b} for infinite values. A uniform limsup bound becomes a uniform bound on the sequences by discarding finitely many terms and allowing any $C>B$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:HI-brai}
If $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$, the ideal $\mathcal{SS}(X)$ and its quotient by $\mathcal K(X)$ admit bounded right approximate identities.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
For a finite family $A_1,\ldots,A_r\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$, choose $L\ge1$ with $\|A_j\|\le L$. The map $Qx=L^{-1}(A_1x,\ldots,A_rx)$ into the finite $\ell_\infty$-sum of copies of $X$ is a strictly singular contraction. For $\delta>0$ fixed, the finite comparison bound and \eqref{eq:HI-exact} give $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$ with
\[
 \|I-S\|<\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)+\delta,
 \qquad \max_j\|A_j-A_jS\|<L(\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)+\delta)\varepsilon.
\]
Direct the choices by finite families and required precision. They give a right approximate identity of norm at most $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)+\delta+1$. Its image in the quotient has the same property.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:HI-cosingular}
Suppose $X$ is H.I. and $\mathcal{SS}(X)\subset\mathcal{SC}(X)$. For every closed $M$ of infinite dimension and codimension, the identity into
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HI-quotientnorm}
 |x|_{\varepsilon,M}=\max\{\varepsilon\|x\|,\operatorname{dist}(x,M)\}
\end{equation}
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HI-radius-one}
 \operatorname{in}(J_{\varepsilon,M})=\varepsilon,
 \qquad d_+(J_{\varepsilon,M})=1\quad(0<\varepsilon\le1).
\end{equation}
Consequently $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The first equality also follows directly from $q_M|_M=0$ and the floor in the norm. For every $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$, $\|q_M-q_MS\|\ge1$. Indeed, if this norm were $r<1$, the isometry $q_M^*$ would give
\[
 \|(q_MS)^*f\|\ge(1-r)\|f\|\quad(f\in(X/M)^*).
\]
An operator whose adjoint is bounded below is surjective, contradicting the strict cosingularity of $S$. Formula~\eqref{eq:HI-exact} now gives $d_+\ge1$. The choice $S=0$ gives $d_+\le1$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:HI-GM}
Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-cosingular} applies if $X$ is H.I. and quotient indecomposable, or if both $X$ and $X^*$ are H.I. In particular, it applies to the original Gowers--Maurey space.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
A space is quotient indecomposable if none of its quotients is a topological direct sum of two closed infinite-dimensional subspaces. For such a range, each endomorphism is either lower semi-Fredholm or strictly cosingular \cite[Theorem 4.3]{G07}. The preceding fact excludes the first alternative for a strictly singular $S$.

If $X^*$ is H.I., the same fact and semi-Fredholm duality imply that $S^*$ is not upper semi-Fredholm. Thus $S^*$ is strictly singular by \eqref{eq:HI-distance} on $X^*$. A surjection $q_MS$ onto an infinite-dimensional quotient would make $S^*q_M^*$ bounded below, which is impossible. Hence $S$ is strictly cosingular.

Ferenczi proved that the original Gowers--Maurey space is quotient hereditarily indecomposable, and that its dual is H.I. \cite[Corollaries 21 and 22]{Fer99}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:HI-small-dual}
Let $X$ be complex H.I. If every endomorphism of $X^*$ is a scalar multiple of the identity plus a strictly singular operator, then \eqref{eq:HI-radius-one} holds. This includes the complex H.I. examples of Ferenczi whose duals are not H.I. \cite[Propositions 23--25]{Fer99}.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
For $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$ write $S^*=\mu I+V$ with $V$ strictly singular. If $\mu\ne0$, $S^*$ and hence $S$ would be Fredholm, a contradiction. Thus $S^*$ is strictly singular, implying that $S$ is strictly cosingular as in the preceding proof. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-cosingular}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:HI-nonSC}
If an H.I. space $X$ has $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$, then for each $M$ of infinite dimension and codimension there are bounded $S_n\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$ with
\[
 \|(I-S_n^*)|_{M^\perp}\|\longrightarrow0.
\]
For all sufficiently large $n$, $S_n^*$ is bounded below on $M^\perp$ and $q_MS_n$ is surjective. In particular $\mathcal{SS}(X)\not\subset\mathcal{SC}(X)$, and $X^*$ is not H.I.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Use Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-quotients} and the isometry of $q_M^*$ onto $M^\perp$. For large $n$, $\|(I-S_n^*)|_{M^\perp}\|<1$, so $S_n^*q_M^*$ is bounded below. Surjectivity follows by adjoint duality. The last assertion follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:HI-GM}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:HI-separation}
For the contraction $Q$ in \eqref{eq:HI-graph}, if
\[
 \delta_Q=\inf_{S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)}\|Q-QS\|>0,
\]
then $d_+(J_{\varepsilon,Q})\ge\delta_Q$ and $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$. It suffices that $Q$ be non-compact and $QS$ compact for every $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The first conclusion is \eqref{eq:HI-exact}. In the sufficient case, $\delta_Q\ge\operatorname{dist}(Q,\mathcal K(X,Z))>0$, because the compact ideal is norm closed.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:HI-nilpotent}
Let $X$ be H.I. If every product of $m$ strictly singular endomorphisms is compact for some $m\ge1$, then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
If $\mathcal{SS}(X)=\mathcal K(X)$, then $\mathcal{SS}(X)\subset\mathcal{SC}(X)$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-cosingular} applies. Otherwise choose the largest length $k$ of a non-compact product. Such a $k$ exists and $1\le k\le m-1$. Choose $Q_0=S_1\cdots S_k$ non-compact. It is strictly singular, and $Q_0S$ is compact for every $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$, by maximality. Normalize $Q=Q_0/\|Q_0\|$ and apply Proposition~\ref{prop:HI-separation} with $Z=X$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:HI-reflexive-ideal}
If $X$ is H.I. and the Banach space $A=\mathcal{SS}(X)/\mathcal K(X)$ is reflexive, then $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$. In particular, this holds whenever the Calkin algebra $\mathcal L(X)/\mathcal K(X)$ is finite-dimensional.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Suppose $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:HI-brai}, $A$ has a bounded right approximate identity $(e_\alpha)$. Reflexivity gives a weakly convergent subnet with limit $e\in A$. For each $a\in A$, bounded linearity of left multiplication and $ae_\alpha\to a$ in norm give $ae=a$. In particular $e^2=e$.

Choose $S\in\mathcal{SS}(X)$ representing $e$. The operator $I-S$ is Fredholm, so $1-e$ is invertible in the full Calkin algebra by Atkinson's theorem. But $e(1-e)=0$, hence $e=0$. Since $ae=a$ for all $a$, this forces $A=0$ and $\mathcal{SS}(X)=\mathcal K(X)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-cosingular} then contradicts finiteness. The finite-dimensional assertion follows because $A$ is a closed subspace of the Calkin algebra.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:HI-examples}
The constant $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}$ is infinite on the Argyros--Haydon space, on every closed infinite-dimensional subspace of the real Argyros--Motakis space $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{ISP}}$, and on every closed infinite-dimensional subspace of the real H.I. spaces constructed in \cite{AM16}.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The scalar-plus-compact property of Argyros--Haydon \cite{AH11}, in either scalar field \cite{KL17}, gives $\mathcal{SS}(X)=\mathcal K(X)$: a non-zero scalar multiple of $I$ plus a compact operator is Fredholm and cannot be strictly singular. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-cosingular}.

For $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{ISP}}$, Argyros--Motakis show that every infinite-dimensional closed subspace is H.I. and every product of three strictly singular endomorphisms on it is compact \cite[Introduction, theorem, (i); Theorem 5.19]{AM14}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-nilpotent} with $m=3$. Their strictly singular ideals contain non-compact operators, so this case is distinct from scalar-plus-compact. The real H.I. constructions in \cite[Theorems 6.13 and 8.4]{AM16} have compact products of two strictly singular operators, also on their closed subspaces; use $m=2$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:HI-dual}
With $1/0=\infty$,
\[
 b_X(M)=\frac1{\eta_X(M)},
 \qquad \Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\frac1{\inf_{M\in\mathcal S(X)}\eta_X(M)}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The operators $R=I-S$ with $S$ strictly singular are exactly those satisfying $\varphi(R)=1$. For a bounded admissible sequence $R_n$ and $f\in E_M^*$,
\[
 1\le\|\varphi-F_M^*f\|\|R_n\|+\|f\|\|F_MR_n\|.
\]
Taking the limit and then the infimum over $f$ gives $1\le\eta_X(M)\limsup\|R_n\|$. This proves the lower bound and the assertion when $\eta_X(M)=0$.

If $\eta=\eta_X(M)>0$, Hahn--Banach gives $u\in B^{**}$ with $\|u\|=1$, $u|_{D_M}=0$ and $u(\varphi)=\eta$. Set $v=u/\eta$. Then $F_M^{**}v=0$ and $v(\varphi)=1$. Goldstine gives a net $A_\alpha$ in the ball of $B$ of radius $1/\eta$, converging weak-star to $v$. The pairs $(F_MA_\alpha,\varphi(A_\alpha)-1)$ converge weakly to zero in $E_M\oplus\mathbb C$. By equality of weak and norm closures for convex sets, choose finite convex combinations $B_n$ with
\[
 \|B_n\|\le1/\eta,\qquad \|F_MB_n\|\to0,\qquad \varphi(B_n)\to1.
\]
Normalize $R_n=B_n/\varphi(B_n)$ for large $n$. These operators are admissible and $\limsup\|R_n\|\le1/\eta$. This proves the first equality; Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-quotients} gives the second.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:HI-distortion}
Tomczak--Jaegermann proved that every H.I. space is arbitrarily distortable \cite[Corollary 3]{TJ96}. For an equivalent norm, its distortion is
\[
 \Delta_X(|\cdot|)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal S(X)}
 \frac{\sup_{x\in M,\ \|x\|=1}|x|}{\inf_{x\in M,\ \|x\|=1}|x|}.
\]
Large distortion does not itself estimate the extension cost in Proposition~\ref{prop:extension}. Conversely, every graph norm \eqref{eq:HI-graph} has $\Delta_X(|\cdot|_{\varepsilon,Q})=1$: on an infinite-dimensional subspace where $\|Q\|<\varepsilon$, it equals $\varepsilon\|\cdot\|$. Hence the exact divergence $d_+/\operatorname{in}=1/\varepsilon$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-cosingular} occurs with distortion one. Persistent distortion is not necessary for this obstruction. Martin\'on \cite{Mar10} studies the relation between distortion and supermultiplicative operational quantities; the quotient argument above uses the surjectivity properties of $q_MS$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
\label{prob:HI}
Is $\sup_{M\in\mathcal S(X)}b_X(M)=\infty$ for every H.I. space $X$? Equivalently, is $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$ for every such domain? A finite value would require the quotient-surjectivity phenomenon in Corollary~\ref{cor:HI-nonSC} and a bounded right approximate identity in the non-reflexive, non-nilpotent quotient ideal $\mathcal{SS}(X)/\mathcal K(X)$. Over $\mathbb C$, it would require $\inf_M\eta_X(M)>0$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:HI-dual}. More generally, is $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)=\infty$ whenever $X$ has an infinite-dimensional subspace containing no uniformly subprojective subspace?
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- problem-3: body_md -->
\label{prob:Lp}
Is $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(L_p(0,1))$ finite for $1<p<2$? These spaces are not subprojective \cite{OiSp15}, but the lifting principle used in Section~\ref{sec:converse} is specific to $\mathcal L_1$-spaces. For $2\le p<\infty$, $L_p(0,1)$ is uniformly subprojective \cite[Remark 2.11]{OiSp15}; determine $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(L_p(0,1))$, which equals $1$ for $p=2$.
<!-- end problem-3 -->
<!-- problem-4: body_md -->
\label{prob:Linfty}
Determine the $\mathcal L_\infty$-spaces with $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(X)<\infty$. For instance, is $\Lambda_{\mathrm{SF}}^{\mathrm{all}}(C[0,1])=\infty$?
<!-- end problem-4 -->
<!-- problem-5: body_md -->
For which infinite-dimensional Banach spaces $Y$ is there a finite constant $C_Y$ such that $d_-^{X,Y}(T)\le C_Y\operatorname{in}_-(T)$ for all domains $X$ and all $T:X\to Y$? Does a corresponding geometric characterization hold for $\mathcal L_\infty$ targets?
<!-- end problem-5 -->
